GUIDE FOR TESTING SINGLE-PHASE AC AND UWVERSAL MOTORS
0. FOREWOliD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 22 August 1974, after the draft finalized by the Rotating Machinery Sectional Committee had been approved by the Electrotechmcal Dition Council. 0.2 The performance requircmenwof single-phase ac and universal motors are covered by IS : 996-1964*. This standard has been-prepared to provide guidance on the test methods for conducting the tests for single-phase ac and universal motors. 0.3 This guide covers methods for conducting the generally applicable tests to determine the performance characteristics of single-phase mot&x. It is not intended that the standard shall cover all possible tests used in production or tests of research nature. The guide shall not be deemed as making it obligatory to carry out any or all the tests specified in this standard. 0.4 In preparing publications : thii guide, assistance has been derived from the following

IS : 4029-1967 Guide for testing three-phase induction motors. AIEE Publication IEEE No.. 114-19.58 Test procedure for single-phase induction motors. The Institute of Electrical and EJectron& Engineers, New York, USA. NEMA Standard M.G. 1 Frame assignments for alternating-cut-rent Integral horse-power induction motors. National Electrical Manufacturers Association, New York, USA. 0.5 In reporting the result of a test made in accordance with ti stan&%rd, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be do x in accordance with IS : 2-196Ot.

1. SCOPE 1.P This guide covers methods for conducting the tests for singlt-phase ac and unive&l motors covered by IS : 996-1964'.

3.1 Instrument S&&i& -- The indicating instruments used in electrical measurements shah conform to IS : 1248-196811. The working range of instruments used shall be so selected as to give indication well up the scale; that is, where a fraction of division is easily estimated and where such a fraction is a small percentage of the value read. 3.2 Instramcnt Transformers - When current and potential transformers are used, corrections shall be made for ratio errors in current and voltage measurements and for ratio and phase angle errors in power meaThe use of instrument transformers shall be avoided if possible. surements. 3.3 Voltage -. -Method of High Voltage Test

6.2.1 ?`he test shall be made with alternating voltage of any convenient frequenq., preferably between 40 and 60 Hz. The test voltage shall be of approximately sine-wave form and, duririg the application of voltage, the peak value, as would be determined by spark gap, by oscillograph or by any other approved method, shall be not more than 1.45 times the rms value. The rms value of the applied voltage shall be measured by means of a voltmeter used with a suitable calibrated potential transformer or by means of voltmeter used in connection with a special calibrated voltmeter winding or testing transformers, or by any other suitable voltmeter connected to the output side of the testing transformer.

6.2.1.1 It is generally advisable that the high voltage test should not be applied if insulation resistance is less than that specified in the relevant equipment specification.
6.2.2 Duration of High Voltage Test (Ty@ Test) - The test shall be commenced at a voltage of about one-third of the test voltage which shall be increased to the full test voltage in accordance with 6.1 as rapidly as is consistent with its value being indicated by the measuring instrument. The full test voltage shall be maintained for one minute. At the end of this period, the test vohage shall be rapidly diminished to one-third of its fulJ value before sxvitching off. 6.2.3 Duration. of the High Voltage Test (Flash Test) (Routine Test) -As routine test, a test voltage equal to the one specified in Table 2 shall be applied between the Tvinding and the frame of the motor, with the core connected to the frame and the windings not under test for 5 seconds. 6.2.4 Supplenzentary High Voltage Test - If, for any reason, it is desired to conduct additional high voltage tests on a motor which has already passed test in accordance with 6.1 and is installed on site, such additional high with the requirements voltage tests shall be carried out in accordance of 6.1 except that the test voltage shall be 80 percent of the value specified therein. Before applying the supplementary high voltage test, the windings shall be cleaned and the machine thoroughly dried out. 7. RESISTANCE measurements a) b)

7.2 Drop of Potential or Voltmeter-Ammeter Method - In this method, a dc ammeter and a voltmeter shall be used. Simultaueous rcadings of both voltage and current at motor terminals shall be taken when their values have lxxcome steady. The relationship between R, V and I is as follows:

7.2.1 Suitable ranges ,f` instruments shali be chosen so that errors of observations arc reduced o the minimum. For the measurement of potential drop of less than 0.5 yolts, the use of a millivoltmeter is recommended. 7.22 The passage of high current may heat the windings appreciably and thus causes erroneous measurement. It is, therefore, recommended that the current be limited to 50 percent of the rated current of the winding. 7.2.3 Care should be taken to compensate tbr the errors introduced in the measurements by the resistance of leads and contacts. Correction for the current drawn by the voltmeter shall be made if it is appreciable. 7.3 Bridge Method - The resistance above 1 ohm may be determined \vith sufficient accuracy if a Wheatstone bridge is used. Resistance less than 1 ohm shall be measured by Kelvin double bridge, also known as RelvinThompson double bridge. 7.3.1 Wheotstone kbidge Method - In using Wheatstone bridge, the resistance of the ratio arms shall be so selected that the values used correspond as closely as possible to the resistance to be measured; the use of one ohm The values of the resistance thus measured ratio coil should be avoided.

8.2 Locked Rotor Test 8.2.1 IL shoulcl be recognized
that the testing of induction !I nwtors under

IS : 7572 - 1974 locked rotor conditions involves unusual mechanical stresses and high rates of heating. Therefore, it is necessary that: a) the mechanical means of locking the rotor be of adequate strength to prevent possible injury to personnel or damage to equipment. b) the direction of rotation be determined prior to this test. c) the current and torque readings be taken at approximately rated voltage and at rated frequency and that the motor be at approsiThe voltage shall be within 5 percent mately ambient temperature. The ammeter reading, shall be corrected by of rated voltage. multiplying it by the rated voltage and dividing the product by the The ammeter shall be voltage read when the ammeter was read. read after its pointer has stopped its periodic swinging but all readings shall be taken within 3 seconds a&J the line slvitch is closed. The tcmperaturc- at the start of every test \hall be not less than 20�C nor more than 40�C.

8.3.1 C;em~-nl -~--Thr speed-torque characteristic is the relation l~t~veeri torque and speed; embracing the range fi,oln zero to synchronous speed. This relation, when expressed as a curve, includes pull out (maximum running:; torque, puh-up (minimum. running, j torque, and locked rotor torque of induction motors (see Fig. 2). The speed-current characteristic is the relation between current and speed. (This CLI~VF:is generally plotted on the same sheet as the speed-torque curve, using a common speed scale for both curves.) The test should be carried out when temperature conditions are stabilized. 8.3.1.1 The speed-torque and speed-current tests may bc made with a dynamometer or by rope and pulley methods. Measurements of current, voltage and speed shall be made. Data for these characteristics shall be taken at or near ratrd voltage. 8.32 Switchitzg Turque --- The switching torque of a motor which has an automatic connection change at some instant in its starting interval is the minimum external torque developed by the motor as it accelerates through switch operating speed. It should be noted that if the torque on the starting connectidn is never less than the switching torque, the pull-up torque is 10

8.3.2.1 ,The procedure :

switching

ma) i be dcterminetl

by the followirl:

The motor is ai!o\ved to run at no load and the torque load is gradually increased until the speed falls off abruptly and the starting switch recloses. With this t orque setting the motor may either fall off in speed or `pump', that is, the speed may cycle between the upper and lower spa& In either case, the torque Ioad should be reduced until the motor transfers and remains on the running connection. An alternative method is to start the motor from rest \vith a heavy load and then gradually decrease the torque until the motor transfers and remains on the running connections.
8.3.3 Pu&Qat Torque - This test may be made by allowing the motor to run light and then increasing the torque until the speed of the motor falls off abruptly. This test should be made as rapidly as is possible, consistent with accuracy, hut not so rapidly as to introduce inertia errors into the readings. 8.3.4 P&o;(, Torque --- The pull-up torque of an alternating current motor is the minimum external torque developed by the motor during the period of acceleration from rest to the speed at which pull-out torque occurs. For motors which do not have a definite pull-out torque, the pull-up torque is the minimum torque developed up to rated speed. 11

8.4.1 Gewal - Load characteristics are obtained by testing a motor as in 8.3 except that the loading is done at least at five points spaced substantiaUy equally from no load to full load and that additional reading of power &put and power factor Shall be taken to calculate efficiency. Readings beyond full load should be taken as far as possible in the same fashion. It should be ensured that the testing at overload shall not cause injury to the motor. This test shall be carried out at rated or mean voltage and rated frequency. 8.4.2

Methods

ofLoading

-

The following methods are recommended.

8.4.2.1 Brake method- In this method, a brake is mounted on the motor shaft and so arranged that a scale reads the retarding force o&red by the brake. The torque is computed from the product of the scale reading and the brake arm length. Care shall be exercised in the construction and use of the brake and the brake pulley. 8.4.2.2 Dynamomcti method - In this method, the motor is connected to a dynamometer usually by means of flexible coupling. The dynamometer is free to rotate and has a torque arm which rests on a scale. The torque output of the motor is a product of the scale reading and the distance from the centre of the dynamometer to the point where the torque arm makes contact with the scale. To obtain the mechanical power output of a motor by the dynamometer method, the following formula may be used: Power in P = T x,r5e;rvmin where

P = rated output in kW, and
T = torque in Nm. 8.4.2.3 Rope and pulley method - In this method, a small rope or cord suspended from a spring scale is wrapped around the motor pulley a sufficient number of times so that when the cord is tightened by a small pull on its free end, the scale measures the motor's pull. If the cord is properly adjusted with negligible tension in the free end, the motor just pulls through the rnlnimum torque points and the scale swing is slow enough so that even This method may the minimum torque in one slow revolution is obtained. be used to test a motor under load, also, if the motor power output is not 12

IS : 7572- 1974
great enough to damage the cord. conditions shall be fulfilled : To obtain accurate results, the following

4

No force may be exerted on the free end of the cord unless the magnitude of the force is known and a correction for it is made. A distinct curvature in the free end of the cord as it leaves the pulley is the only conclusive evidence that there is no force.

The pulley face should be wide enough to develop the required torque with a single layer of turns of cord. If a single layer is not practicable; multiple layers may be used but the first two turn< on the scale end of 111~cord shall be single layer. cj The pulley shall be in proper alignment with the scale so that there is no scale error caused by a non-recording component ot f&e in the cord. The alignment shall also be such that there, is a clearance l)el\vec:n &c cord and the pullel- flange. 8.4.2.4 applied : C,brrections fo he appfied -- The following corrections shall 1~

a), For cord diameter (see 8.4.2.3) -.- In calculating the torque, the radius at which the force applied is to be taken shall be the pullc): radiuc plus half the thickness of the cord. The cord diameter should br measured with the cord under tension. The micrometer anvil and spindle should have flat faces large enough to span at least t\vo strand pitches. Sufficient pressure should be applied to flatten minor irregularities in the cord. In as much as the cord diameter may change because of wear or stretch, the ratio of cord diameter to pulley diameter should be as small as practicable. b) For pulley wtndape loss and for dynamometer windage loss (see 8.4.2.2 and 8.4.2.3)`fhe measured values of torque are to be corrected 1,) adding to them a torque corresponding to the pullev windage or the The allowance for th& loss is made by dynamometer windage loss. adding a torque l;v :

8.5.3.1 For motors with continuous rating, the tehnperature-rise test Whenever should be continued till thermal equilibrium has been reached. possible, the temperature should be measured both while running and after shut down. 8.5.3.2 For motors with short time rating, the duration of the test should correspond to the declared short time rating. The commonly used methods for measuring temperature are listed below. It may be desirable to use one of these as a check on another : a) Thermometer method (using liquid-in-glass thermometer, resistance thermometer or thermocouple) ; bj Applied thermocouple method; and c) Resistance method. The thermometer method is usually not as accurate as the OLIIC~ two methods for measuring temperatures in small fractional horsepower motors because of the difficulties encountered in properly placing the thermometer. Furthermore, thermocouples do not conduct away as much of the coil heat as thermometers do. The applied thermocouple method is quite often used in conjunction with either the thermometer or resistance method. thermometers, before 8.5.6.1 Thermometer method --- Liquid-in-glass When the therbeing used should be examined for broken liquid columns. mometer is in position, the level of its bulb shall not be higher than that 01 its stern. The bulb should be secured in position with a felt pad, a small piece of putty, or the equivalent, in such a manner as to shield it from the surrounding air. There should be restriction of the natural windage oC the motor or of the heat radiation from the coil of which the temperature is being measured. The liquid-in-glass thermometer, resistance thermometer, or thermocouple are applied to the hottest parts accessible without alteration of the structure. The temperature shall be measured on the surface ot` the coil ends at two peripherily spaced locations. 8.5.6.2 Applied thermocouple method -- In using this method, thcrmocouples are applied to the conductor insulation in the hottest parts acceGblc to them. After being well tucked in, they arc covered with a small picctr of putty or modelling clay. 8.5.6.3 ResistamP method ~- The average temperature throughout a motor winding is determined by comparing the resistancr of the winding at the temperature to be determined with the resistance at a known temperature. 8.5.9.2 Cooling air temperature for temperature-rise test - A motor may be tested at any convenient value of cooling medium temperature less than 40�C but whatever the value of this cooling medium temperature, the pcrmissiblc rise of temperature shall not exceed, during the test, those specified in the relevant equipment specification. In the case of motors intended to operate under conditions in which tht maximum cooling air temperature exceeds 40�C the temperature-rise a\ given in the relevant specification shall be reduced as follows: a) By 5�C if the temperature of the cooling air exceeds 40�C by 5�C or less; 1,) By 10�C if the temperature of the cooling air exceeds 40�C by more than 5�C but not more than 10�C; and c) By agreement, if the temperature of the cooling air is more than 10�C above 40�C. Tests of temperature-rise may be carried out at any convenient cooling air temperature.
